subsection.title: Continuous Functions
subsection.paragraph: Continuous functions will play an important role throughout most of our study of calculus. Loosely speaking, a function is continuous at a point if the graph of the function at that point is devoid of holes, gaps, jumps, or breaks. Consider, for example, the graph of the function $$f$$ depicted in Figure 39.

subsection.paragraph: Let’s take a closer look at the behavior of $$f$$ at or near $$x = a$$ , $$x = b$$ , $$x = c$$ , and $$x = d$$ . First, note that $$f$$ is not defined at $$x = a$$ ; that is, $$x = a$$ is not in the domain of $$f$$ , thereby resulting in a “hole” in the graph of $$f$$ . Next, observe that the value of $$f$$ at $$b$$ , $$f(b)$$ , is not equal to the limit of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$b$$ , resulting in a “jump” in the graph of $$f$$ at $$x = b$$ . The function $$f$$ does not have a limit at $$x = c$$ since the left-hand and right-hand limits of $$f(x)$$ are not equal, also resulting in a jump in the graph of $$f$$ at $$x = c$$ . Finally, the limit of $$f$$ does not exist at $$x = d$$ , resulting in a break in the graph of $$f$$ . The function $$f$$ is discontinuous at each of these numbers. It is continuous everywhere else.

If $$f$$ is not continuous at $$x = a$$ , then $$f$$ is said to be discontinuous at $$x = a$$ . Also, $$f$$ is continuous on an interval if $$f$$ is continuous at every number in the interval.

item.paragraph: The function $$f$$ is continuous everywhere because the three conditions for continuity are satisfied for all values of $$x$$ .
The function $$g$$ is discontinuous at $$x = 2$$ because $$g$$ is not defined at that number. It is continuous everywhere else.

The function $$h$$ is discontinuous at $$x = 2$$ because the third condition for continuity is violated; the limit of $$h(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ exists and has the value $$4$$ , but this limit is not equal to $$h(2) = 1$$ . It is continuous for all other values of $$x$$ .
The function $$F$$ is continuous everywhere except at $$x = 0$$ , where the limit of $$F(x)$$ fails to exist as $$x$$ approaches zero (see Example 3a, Section 2.4).
Since the limit of $$G(x)$$ does not exist as $$x$$ approaches zero, we conclude that $$G$$ fails to be continuous at $$x = 0$$ . The function $$G$$ is continuous everywhere else.

subsection.title: Properties of Continuous Functions
subsection.paragraph: The following properties of continuous functions follow directly from the definition of continuity and the corresponding properties of limits. They are stated without proof.

item.paragraph: The constant function $$f(x) = c$$ is continuous everywhere.
The identity function $$f(x) = x$$ is continuous everywhere.

paragraph.em: If f and g are continuous at x = a , then

item.paragraph: $$\left\lbrack f(x)\rbrack^{n} \right.$$ , where $$n$$ is a real number, is continuous at $$x = a$$ whenever it is defined at that number.
$$f \slash g$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ provided that $$g(a) \neq 0$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Using these properties of continuous functions, we can prove the following results. (A proof is sketched in Exercise 101)

note.title: Continuity of Polynomial and Rational Functions

item.paragraph: A polynomial function $$y = P(x)$$ is continuous at every value of $$x$$ .
A rational function $$R(x) = p(x) \slash q(x)$$ is continuous at every value of $$x$$ where $$q(x) \neq 0$$ .

To put it another way, the train cannot occupy the positions $$s_{1}$$ and $$s_{2}$$ without at least, at some time, occupying an intermediate position (Figure 43).

subsection.paragraph: This discussion carries the gist of the Intermediate Value Theorem. The proof of this theorem can be found in most advanced calculus texts.

subsection.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem
subsection.paragraph: If $$f$$ is a continuous function on a closed interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ and $$M$$ is any number between $$f(a)$$ and $$f(b)$$ , then there is at least one number $$c$$ in $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ such that $$f(c) = M$$ (Figure 45).

To illustrate the Intermediate Value Theorem, let’s look at the example involving the motion of the maglev again (see Figure 27). Notice that the initial position of the train is $$f(0) = 0$$ and the position at the end of its test run is $$f(10) = 400$$ . Furthermore, the function $$f$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack 0,10\rbrack$$ . So the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that if we arbitrarily pick a number between $$0$$ and $$400$$ —say, $$100$$ —giving the position of the maglev, there must be a $$\overline{t}$$ (read “$$t$$ bar”) between $$0$$ and $$10$$ at which time the train is at the position $$s = 100$$ . To find the value of $$\overline{t}$$ , we solve the equation $$f\left( \overline{t} \right) = s$$ , or
giving $$\overline{t} = 5$$ ($$t$$ must lie between $$0$$ and $$10$$ ).

It is important to remember when we use Theorem 4 that the function $$f$$ must be continuous. The conclusion of the Intermediate Value Theorem may not hold if $$f$$ is not continuous (see Exercise 102).

The next theorem is an immediate consequence of the Intermediate Value Theorem. It not only tells us when a zero of a function $$f$$ [root of the equation $$f(x) = 0$$ ] exists but also provides the basis for a method of approximating it.

subsection.title: Existence of Zeros of a Continuous Function
subsection.paragraph: If $$f$$ is a continuous function on a closed interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ , and if $$f(a)$$ and $$f(b)$$ have opposite signs, then there is at least one solution of the equation $$f(x) = 0$$ in the interval $$(a,b)$$ (Figure 46).

Geometrically, this property states that if the graph of a continuous function goes from above the $$x$$ -axis to below the $$x$$ -axis or vice versa, it must cross the $$x$$ -axis. This is not necessarily true if the function is discontinuous (Figure 47).
